bibl.title: Stochastic Variational Inference
bibl.publisher: Journal of Machine Learning Research / arXiv

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: We develop stochastic variational inference, a scalable algorithm for approximating posterior distributions.

span.label: scalable approximate posterior inference in hierarchical Bayesian models
span.quote: Inference algorithms of the 1990s and 2000s used to be considered scalable, but they cannot easily handle the amount of data that we described in the four examples above.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: We develop this technique for a large class of probabilistic models and we demonstrate it with two probabilistic topic models, latent Dirichlet allocation and the hierarchical Dirichlet process topic model.

span.label: The general algorithm is derived only for conjugate exponential-family models and does not cover nonconjugate models such as correlated or dynamic topic models.
span.quote: We developed our algorithm with conjugate exponential family models.

span.label: Convergence is only to a local optimum, and very small minibatches can lead to a poor one.
span.quote: Stochastic variational inference is guaranteed to converge to a local optimum but taking large steps on the basis of very few data points may lead to a poor one.

span.label: The quality of the solution and speed of convergence depend on how the forgetting rate, delay and minibatch size are set.
span.quote: Although stochastic variational inference algorithm converges to a stationary point for any valid κ, τ , and S, the quality of this stationary point and the speed of convergence may depend on how these parameters are set.

span.label: What is optimised is a bound standing in for a quantity the method cannot compute.
span.quote: Since we cannot compute p(x | α) exactly, an approximate approach is to maximize the fitted variational lower bound

span.label: A prior is made exchangeable for simplicity, and the paper notes the conditional then is not.
span.quote: but for simplicity we assume exchangeable Dirichlet priors; that is, we require that all of these parameters are set to the same value

span.label: The evaluation is built from a split of each test document's words, constructed to be disjoint.
span.quote: we divide each test document’s words w into a set of observed words wobs and held-out words who, keeping the sets of unique words in wobs and who disjoint

span.label: How many topics a collection needs is answered by the model's own posterior.
span.quote: Given a collection of documents, the posterior distribution of the hidden structure determines how many topics are needed to describe them

span.label: a topic - A WEIGHTED DISTRIBUTION OVER THE VOCABULARY: not a subject, a theme or an aboutness, but a probability vector over words, shown to a reader by printing its most frequent members - which is why a multi-word name has no way to stay together inside one
span.quote: Each topic is a weighted distribution over the vocabulary and each topic’s plot illustrates its most frequent words

span.label: topic proportions - A DISTRIBUTION OVER TOPICS, so a distribution over distributions: the same word does duty at two levels in one sentence, and a document's 'topics' are weights on objects that are themselves weights on words
span.quote: Each document in the collection is associated with a vector of topic proportions θd, which is a distribution over topics

span.label: the ELBO - A LOWER BOUND SUBSTITUTED FOR THE THING WANTED: the algorithm maximises a bound on the log marginal probability rather than that probability, and the gap between them is not reported because computing it would require the quantity the bound exists to avoid
span.quote: It maximizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO), a lower bound on the logarithm of the marginal probability of the observations

span.label: builds-on → the Robbins and Monro (1951) stochastic approximation method
span.quote: In this paper, we develop scalable methods for generic Bayesian inference by solving the variational inference problem with stochastic optimization (Robbins and Monro, 1951).
